tip: There's no 'to open' in Greek – you say 'I want that I open': θέλω να ανοίξω (thelo na anixo). English to-verbs all become να plus a fully conjugated verb.
Greek's question mark is the semicolon – that final ; is it. No word-order flip either: Μπορώ να κλείσω (boro na kliso = can I close) stays statement-shaped; tone does the asking.
You lift money from an ATM: σήκωσα λεφτά (sikosa lefta = I lifted money). Σηκώνω (sikono), the verb for picking things up, is the everyday word for withdrawing cash.
You 'make' a card in Greek: να κάνω μια χρεωστική κάρτα (na kano mia chreostiki karta). The same κάνω (kano) covers applications and licenses too.
Clock times are plural: στις οκτώ (stis okto) – literally 'at the eights', short for 'at the eight hours'. Only one o'clock is singular: στη μία (sti mia).
Υπάλληλος (ipallilos) is one word for both genders – only the article shows who it is: η υπάλληλος (i ipallilos) is a woman, ο υπάλληλος a man.
Μου έκοψαν (mou ekopsan = they cut on me) – no 'they' word appears. Greek uses a bare plural verb for companies and authorities; the μου (mou) marks who it hit.
Δεν (den) and τίποτα (tipota) stack: δεν μου έμεινε τίποτα (den mou emine tipota = nothing was left to me). Greek requires the double negative – one negative alone is a mistake.
Money is plural in Greek: τα λεφτά δεν φτάνουν (ta lefta den ftanoun) – literally 'the moneys don't reach'. Articles and verbs with λεφτά (lefta) always go plural.
Τον άλλο μήνα (ton allo mina) – literally 'the other month' – means NEXT month, not some other one. Same trick: την άλλη βδομάδα (tin alli vdomada) = next week.
The object pronoun goes before the verb in statements: την ακύρωσα (tin akirosa = it I-canceled). Only commands flip it: ακύρωσέ την (akirose tin).
After να (na), 'not' is μη (mi), never δεν (den): να μη χρωστάς (na mi chrostas = that you not owe). Δεν (den) is for plain statements only.
'Per day' has no 'per' – just 'the day': τη μέρα (ti mera). Rates all work this way: δύο φορές τη βδομάδα (dio fores ti vdomada) = twice a week.
Τα βγάζουμε πέρα (ta vgazoume pera) – literally 'we get them across' – is THE phrase for making ends meet. The τα (ta) points to nothing specific; it's baked into the idiom.
Saved money goes 'to the edge': βάζω λίγα λεφτά στην άκρη (vazo liga lefta stin akri = I put a little money at the edge) = set aside. Greek's standard image for saving.
Λογαριασμός (logariasmos) is both 'bank account' and 'bill' – here τον λογαριασμό του ρεύματος (ton logariasmo tou revmatos) is the electricity bill. Context decides which.
Greek commands mark duration: πάρε (pare) = take, one-off; περίμενε (perimene) = keep waiting, ongoing. A different verb stem for once vs continuing.
Χρειάζεστε (chriazeste) is plural 'you need' aimed at one person – Greek politeness uses the plural, like French vous. Expect it from clerks and officials.
Δεν προλάβαινα να πληρώσω (den prolavena na pliroso) = I didn't manage to pay in time. Προλαβαίνω (prolaveno) packs 'have time to' into one verb – no 'time' word needed.
'Than' before a clause is απ' ό,τι (ap' o,ti): πιο γρήγορα απ' ό,τι περίμενα (pio grigora ap' o,ti perimena = faster than I expected). Plain από (apo) fits only before nouns.
